sections.h2: Where is Petersburg, Virginia, and how is the city laid out?
sections.html:
Petersburg is an independent city about 21 miles south of Richmond, on the Appomattox River at the fall line where Virginia's Piedmont meets the coastal plain. The city covers roughly 23 square miles, and the Census Bureau puts its 2025 population estimate at 33,734.

It sits where Interstate 95 and Interstate 85 meet, which is why so many Petersburg owners are a short drive from jobs in Richmond, Colonial Heights, Hopewell and the Fort Lee area. Petersburg belongs to the Richmond-Petersburg metropolitan area, and neighboring Dinwiddie and Prince George counties wrap around it.

Because Petersburg is an independent city, there is no separate county government. The same city offices handle assessment, tax bills, code enforcement and permits, so a seller usually deals with one set of departments instead of two.

sections.h2: What does Petersburg's history mean for an older house?
sections.html:
Many Petersburg homes are old, and some are very old. The town was incorporated in 1748, rebuilt after a large fire in 1815, and shaped by the 1864 and 1865 siege that left the city badly damaged.

Later growth came from tobacco, cotton, flour and iron, plus a string of railroads built before the Civil War. That industrial past left behind brick rowhouses, mill-era housing and large Victorian homes, often with original plaster, old wiring and aging plumbing.

  • Petersburg Old Town Historic District has been on the National Register of Historic Places since July 4, 1980 and covers about 190 acres.
  • Pocahontas Island, one of the oldest free Black settlements in the state, is listed as its own historic district.
  • Battersea, a Palladian house built in 1767 and 1768, stands on the western edge of the city above the river.

If your house is inside a historic area, repairs and exterior changes can involve extra review, which is one reason owners of worn-down older homes look for a buyer who takes the property as it stands.

Petersburg grew as a manufacturing and rail town, and a few of those companies are still here. Arnold Pen Co., Seward Trunk Co., Titmus Optical and Amsted Rail-Brenco are listed among the businesses operating in the city.

Much of the regional hiring now happens just outside the city line. A Walmart distribution center opened west of town in Dinwiddie County in the early 1990s, and an Amazon fulfillment center opened in Dinwiddie County in September 2012. Fort Lee, home to the Army's Sustainment Center of Excellence, is another large federal employer nearby.

Heritage tourism also matters. Civic leaders promote heritage tourism, the National Park Service preserves part of the Petersburg battlefield, and Old Town has seen older buildings turned into restaurants, shops and apartments.

For a seller, this mix means buyers come from several directions: commuters toward Richmond, workers tied to the distribution centers and base, and investors who want to renovate older stock.

sections.h2: How do roads, rail and transit affect Petersburg homes?
sections.html:
Few cities this size have so many ways in and out. Interstates 95 and 85 meet here, the south end of I-295 lies just south of the city, and US 1, US 301 and US 460 all pass through.

  • CSX and Norfolk Southern both keep rail operations in Petersburg.
  • Amtrak serves the area from a station in Ettrick, with Northeast Regional trains to Norfolk.
  • A Greater Richmond Transit Company bus links Petersburg with downtown Richmond, and Petersburg Area Transit serves the local Tri-Cities area.
  • Richmond International Airport is less than 30 miles north.

Location relative to rail lines and the interstate is something buyers weigh, so mention it up front when you describe your house. We look at the property and its surroundings together when we review it.

sections.h2: What does Petersburg's climate mean for a house?
sections.html:
Petersburg has a humid subtropical climate, with hot, muggy summers and mild to cool winters. NOAA normals show a July average high of 89.3 degrees and a January average low of 28.3 degrees.

The area gets about 47 inches of precipitation a year, spread across roughly 115 days with measurable rain or snow. That steady moisture is hard on old roofs, wood trim, crawl spaces and basements, so a house that has sat empty through several humid seasons is worth checking for leaks and moisture before you decide how to sell.

The city also sits on a river at the fall line, so low parcels near the Appomattox deserve a look at flood maps before you list. Ask the city about the status of your specific lot.

sections.h2: What are Petersburg's rules for vacant buildings?
sections.html:
Petersburg requires the owner of a building that has been continuously vacant for 12 months or more to register it with the building code official. A building counts as continuously vacant even if it is occupied now and then during that period (City Code Sec. 22-140).

  • The first registration costs $100, and another non-refundable $100 is due within 15 days of each anniversary while the building stays vacant.
  • Owners must give the address, owner and agent contact details, an estimate of how long the building will stay vacant and a plan for maintaining it.
  • The owner must also show an ongoing rodent control plan for the inside and outside of the building.
  • Not registering is a civil violation with a $200 penalty, or $400 if the building is in a historic area, a conservation or rehabilitation district, or an area council has declared blighted.

The city mails notice at least 30 days before a penalty is imposed. Questions go to the Housing Inspector at 106 W. Tabb St., 804-733-2410, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. For inherited or empty houses, these fees and penalties are a real carrying cost, and selling ends them.

sections.h2: How does Petersburg assess property and send tax bills?
sections.html:
Petersburg reviews every real estate assessment every two years, using January 1 values. The city says assessments may rise, stay the same or fall depending on the market, changes to the property and corrections.

In a reassessment year, change of assessment notices go out on January 28, and only to owners whose value changed. The notice explains the appeal steps, which are an office review and then the Board of Review.

The January 1 value is used for billing from the following July 1 through June 30. The city lists four due dates: September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30. The assessor also notes that family transfers, foreclosures, bank sales and estate sales may be left out of the sales analysis because they are not treated as arm's-length deals.

If you sell mid-year, ask the closing agent how the current bill will be handled at settlement. Our source for these dates is the city assessor's own page.

sections.h2: What does a seller pay at closing in Petersburg?
sections.html:
Virginia charges a state-level grantor tax of 50 cents for each $500 of the sale price, and it is normally paid by the seller. Under the statute the grantor pays unless the two sides agree the buyer will cover some or all of it, and the deed cannot be recorded until the clerk certifies the tax was paid.

Half of that tax goes to the state and half to the locality. The full text is in Virginia Code 58.1-802. Other closing costs depend on how you sell, and we leave those out because they change by deal.

Ask your closing company for an itemized estimate before you pick a route. A list-and-repair sale and an as-is cash sale produce very different bottom lines.

sections.h2: What do Petersburg sellers usually run into?
sections.html:
Sellers in Petersburg tend to be dealing with a house that is old, vacant or inherited. Typical problems include deferred repairs, a vacancy registration that has to be renewed, back taxes, and heirs who live in other states.

A cash sale works best when time or condition is the issue. You describe the house, we review it, and if an offer makes sense it is based on the property as it is, with no repair list required from you. You can say no, and you owe nothing for asking.

If you are weighing options, compare a traditional listing, a sale to an investor and a cash offer on the same sheet: net proceeds, time to close and what repairs you must pay for first.

faqs.q: How many people live in Petersburg, VA?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimates Petersburg had 33,734 residents on July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 33,458.

faqs.q: Does Petersburg have a vacant property registry?
faqs.a: Yes. A building vacant for 12 months or more must be registered with the building code official, with a $100 annual fee and a $200 penalty ($400 in historic or blighted areas) for not registering.

faqs.q: How often does Petersburg reassess real estate?
faqs.a: Every two years, using values as of January 1. Notices go out January 28 of a reassessment year to owners whose value changed.

faqs.q: When are Petersburg real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: The city lists September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30 as the four due dates for the July 1 through June 30 billing period.

faqs.q: Who pays the Virginia grantor tax when a house sells?
faqs.a: The seller pays it by default, at 50 cents per $500 of the price, unless the buyer and seller agree otherwise.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Petersburg house that needs major repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it as is, and you do not have to fix anything or clean it out first.
